S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
examples: Focuses at first during class or meetings but soon becomes distracted or spaces out.
Re-reads the same paragraph in a book multiple times but the content does not register.
Loses focus while watching movies or TV and misses the plot.
Unable to maintain attention until the end of a long meeting or lecture, often drifting off or becoming drowsy.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
examples: Appears not to be listening, looking elsewhere or spacing out during conversation.
Immediately asks to repeat what was just said or instructed.
Does not respond when name is called or answers only after a long delay.
Misses the content of the conversation, giving unrelated answers or out-of-context reactions.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
examples: Starts homework or projects but fails to complete them, submitting unfinished work or missing deadlines.
When given multi-step instructions, follows only the first few steps and forgets the rest.
Starts cleaning or organizing but switches to another task midway, failing to finish.
Leaves almost completed work reports or paperwork unfinished, neglecting the final steps.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
examples: Frequently loses school supplies or office supplies like pens, erasers, and calculators.
Always searching for glasses, cell phones, wallets, or keys because they do not know where they are.
Loses necessary documents or materials at home or in the office and cannot find them.
Cannot remember where they placed an item they were holding just moments ago.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
examples: Forgets appointment times or meeting schedules, arriving late or missing them entirely.
Forgets to reply to received calls or messages for days.
Frequently incurs late fees because of missing deadlines for utility bills or credit card payments.
Forgets to take medication or leaves necessary items at home when going out.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, Predominantly Inattentive Presentation, is characterized by a persistent pattern of inattention, such as difficulty sustaining focus, organizing tasks, and following through on activities, that leads to clinically significant impairment in functioning for at least six months across settings. Hyperactivity and impulsivity are minimal or absent, distinguishing this presentation from combined or hyperactive-impulsive types. In adults, it often presents as disorganization, mental fatigue with sustained tasks, and chronic inefficiency rather than overt behavioral problems seen in childhood. It must be differentiated from cognitive decline, mood or anxiety disorders, and the effects of medical illness or substances; in adults, symptoms often become more apparent or impairing when life demands for self-management and multitasking increase.

patient.personality: Edward is reserved, intellectually curious, and methodical, with a practical streak and a quiet pride in being well-prepared and reliable.
patient.stressor: As Edward began transitioning from a fast-paced advisory role into a semi-retired 'legacy consulting' arrangement, his days shifted from a tightly structured schedule to a patchwork of part-time client work, museum volunteering, and personal projects. Without the external scaffolding of a traditional workday and an assistant to organize his materials, he found himself setting up new home-based systems for files, devices, and reference books, only to realize he couldn’t reliably keep track of where things were or what he had planned for the afternoon. The freedom of this new phase of life accentuated long-standing but previously compensated tendencies toward mental drifting when he moved between tasks, which now interfered with simple routines like preparing for a docent tour or a client call. After several episodes of misplacing items he considered essential to his identity—like his favorite annotated market texts and his volunteer badge—and feeling uncharacteristically embarrassed in front of clients and museum staff, he agreed with his wife’s suggestion to consult a psychiatrist to understand why everyday organization had become such an unexpected struggle.
patient.chief_complaint: “I keep misplacing the things I need for my day, and it’s starting to interfere with my work and volunteering.”

S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
S002.manifestation: Since I shifted to working from home, I’ve noticed that I’ll sit down to review a client’s portfolio or prep for a museum tour, and after ten minutes my mind just drifts off—I find myself staring out the window or thinking about something else, and I have to keep rereading the same page to take anything in.

S003.name: Listening_Difficulty
S003.description: Often does not seem to listen when spoken to directly.
S003.manifestation: My wife or a client will be telling me something quite straightforward, like a change in plans or a detail about a meeting, and I suddenly realize I’ve caught only half of it because my mind wandered even though I was looking right at them, so I have to ask them to repeat themselves, which is embarrassing at my age.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
S004.manifestation: These days, if I make myself a little list for the afternoon—review a report, answer emails, pull materials for the next tour—I’ll start on the first item but somehow get sidetracked midway, poking at my inbox or a book, and then discover in the evening that I never actually finished the thing I sat down to do.

S007.name: Losing_Items
S007.description: Often loses things necessary for tasks or activities.
S007.manifestation: I used to pride myself on knowing where everything was, but now I’m constantly hunting for my reading glasses, my phone, or a specific binder—like I’ll set my volunteer badge or a client folder down “just for a second” while I make tea, and then spend twenty minutes going room to room trying to remember where I put it.

S009.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
S009.description: Often forgetful in daily activities (e.g., doing chores, running errands; for older adolescents and adults, returning calls, paying bills, keeping appointments).
S009.manifestation: Even with a paper calendar and my phone reminders, I’ve been forgetting simple but important things—returning calls from long-time clients, paying a bill on time, or bringing the right notes to the museum—and I usually only realize I’ve dropped the ball when someone prompts me or I see a late notice.
